position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Evidence shows homeowners are treated for chainsaw injuries (128,000 treated in U.S. emergency departments from 2018-2022), but it does not prove they are motivated by safety concerns or would prefer professional-grade tools. A proposed survey test (X1) is needed to measure homeowner preference for safety-critical versus convenience-focused chainsaws.

frame.objective: Determine whether STIHL should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its chainsaw and outdoor power-tool engineering, based on evidence available up to November 2018.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before November 2018; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Consider the current reach of STIHL to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Alternatives include no expansion, a different route to consumers, a different customer group, or a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., homeowner chainsaw for light landscaping).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation (e.g., broader retail distribution of existing tools).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on professional segments (forestry, agriculture, construction).
4) Partner with or license STIHL technology to third‑party consumer brands for a differentiated product.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they perceive chainsaws as dangerous and fear injury, leading them to prefer professional-grade tools that are sold through dealers and marketed as safety-critical.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners who need chainsaws for light landscaping and are motivated by safety concerns.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of chainsaw-related injuries (e.g., 128,000 treated in U.S. emergency departments from 2018-2022) makes homeowners more risk-averse and less willing to purchase consumer-grade chainsaws.
T1.how_value_is_captured: STIHL can capture value by positioning its professional-grade tools as safety-critical, premium products sold through dealers, allowing higher price points and reduced distribution costs.
assumptions: Homeowners are aware of chainsaw injury statistics and actively seek safety.
Professional-grade tools are perceived as safer than consumer chainsaws.
Dealers can effectively communicate safety benefits to consumers.
predictions: In a survey, homeowners will indicate higher willingness to pay for a chainsaw marketed as safety-critical compared to a generic consumer chainsaw.
Sales of professional-grade chainsaws will increase in regions with higher injury rates.
Homeowners will be less likely to purchase consumer chainsaws if safety concerns are highlighted.

assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay more for tools that save time.
Cordless and electric chainsaws are perceived as more convenient than gas models.
STIHL can adapt its engineering to meet consumer convenience expectations.
predictions: In a survey, homeowners will rank convenience as a top purchase criterion for chainsaws.

Homeowners will be less price-sensitive when convenience is highlighted.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners with experience using chainsaws for landscaping, recruited via panel. Randomly split into two equal groups (250 per group).
X1.measure: 1) Percentage of each group who would purchase a professional-grade chainsaw marketed as safety-critical. 2) Percentage who would purchase a consumer-grade chainsaw marketed as convenient. 3) Average maximum price homeowners would pay for each option.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A (safety-critical) will show ≥15% higher purchase rate than Group B (convenience).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B (convenience) will show ≥15% higher purchase rate than Group A (safety).

X1.decision_rule: If Group A purchase rate ≥15% points above Group B, favour T1 (safety-driven). If Group B purchase rate ≥15% points above Group A, favour T2 (convenience-driven). If neither difference reaches 15%, conclude no strong preference and recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. A proposed survey test (X1) is needed to measure homeowner preference for safety-critical versus convenience-focused chainsaws.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who need chainsaws for light landscaping and are motivated by safety concerns.
final.value_proposition: Professional-grade chainsaws marketed as safety-critical, sold through dealers, allowing premium pricing and reduced distribution costs.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Homeowner Preference Survey for Safety vs Convenience Chainsaws (X1) to test purchase intent differences.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to injury statistics and company claims; no direct consumer demand data is available. The survey test is needed to confirm whether safety concerns drive purchase decisions.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a 15% or greater difference in purchase intent between safety-critical and convenience-focused chainsaws, the recommendation would shift toward the favoured theory.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case at this time. The evidence shows OEMs already capture consumer demand for Intel chips, and there is no public source indicating that home computer buyers in 1991 would pay a premium for a branded Intel product. The test proposed (Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiasts vs OEM Buyers) is the next step to validate this.

frame.objective: Determine whether Intel should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its microprocessors, using evidence available in March 1991.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before March 1991; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Alternatives must include no expansion, different route to consumers, different customer group, and other options not suggested in the question.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home networking, gaming, or mobile computing) using Intel microprocessors.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings to individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales of Intel chips).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on selling microprocessors to computer manufacturers.
4) Partner with consumer electronics manufacturers to co‑develop a consumer product line using Intel chips.
5) Target a new customer segment such as small businesses or hobbyists with specialized hardware solutions.

T1.claim: Home computer buyers in 1991 will not purchase a differentiated Intel consumer product because they view the microprocessor as an OEM component, not a consumer brand, and will buy only the OEM hardware that includes it.
T1.who_benefits: Intel would benefit if it could capture consumer demand through a branded product, but the consumer market is already served by OEMs, so the benefit is indirect.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers decide on the whole system, not just the component, and will not pay a premium for a branded Intel product when the OEM hardware already meets their needs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Value would be captured through premium pricing for a branded product, but the evidence shows OEMs already capture consumer demand, so the mechanism is unlikely.
assumptions: Home computer buyers in 1991 are primarily OEM-driven and do not prioritize brand.
OEMs already meet consumer demand, so a differentiated Intel product would not add value.
Intel's brand is not perceived as a differentiator by consumers.
predictions: A survey of home computer buyers in 1991 would show low willingness to pay a premium for a branded Intel product.
OEMs would continue to be the primary source of consumer demand for Intel chips.
Intel's consumer product would not achieve meaningful market penetration compared to OEM offerings.
T1.first_claim: Home computer buyers in 1991 will not purchase a differentiated Intel consumer product because they view the microprocessor as an OEM component, not a consumer brand, and will buy only the OEM hardware that includes it.

T2.claim: Home computer buyers in 1991 will purchase a differentiated Intel consumer product if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance option for enthusiasts and early adopters, because they value performance and are willing to pay more for it.
T2.who_benefits: Intel would benefit by capturing a niche market of performance-conscious consumers who are willing to pay a premium for advanced features.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Enthusiasts and early adopters seek the latest performance and are willing to pay more for it, creating demand for a differentiated product.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Value is captured through premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales of high-end Intel-based systems, leveraging Intel's performance reputation.
assumptions: A segment of home computer buyers in 1991 is willing to pay a premium for performance.
Intel's brand can be associated with high performance, attracting this segment.
Direct-to-consumer sales can reach this segment effectively.
predictions: A survey of enthusiasts would show higher willingness to pay for a branded Intel product compared to OEM offerings.
Direct-to-consumer sales of Intel-based systems would generate higher revenue than OEM sales.
Intel's consumer product would achieve meaningful market penetration among performance-conscious buyers.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiasts vs OEM Buyers
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from a panel of home computer enthusiasts (1991) and general consumers (1991). Each participant sees a product description of an Intel-based system (e.g., 386SX) and is asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay for it. The survey also asks about brand importance and whether they would purchase from Intel directly.
X1.sample: 200 enthusiasts (estimated 100) and 200 general consumers (estimated 100), balanced across gender and age. Recruitment via online panels, estimated €1,000 for incentives and panel fees.
X1.measure: Average maximum price willingness to pay for the Intel system, and brand importance rating (1-7). Secondary measure: intent to purchase from Intel directly.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Enthusiasts will show lower willingness to pay and lower brand importance than general consumers, consistent with OEM-driven demand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Enthusiasts will show higher willingness to pay and higher brand importance than general consumers, consistent with premium demand.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for enthusiasts is at least 20% lower than for general consumers (i.e., average enthusiast price < 0.8 × average general price), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, conclude no significant difference. If the difference is at least 15 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If the average willingness to pay is the same or near the OEM price, conclude neither theory is supported.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer willingness to pay for a differentiated Intel product. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case at this time. The evidence shows OEMs already capture consumer demand for Intel chips, and there is no public source indicating that home computer buyers in 1991 would pay a premium for a branded Intel product. The proposed test (Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiasts vs OEM Buyers) is the next step to validate this.
final.target_customer: OEMs and general consumers who purchase Intel chips for their computer systems.
final.value_proposition: No value proposition yet; the investment would be justified only if a differentiated consumer product achieved meaningful market penetration, which is not supported by the evidence.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (or a similar test) to measure consumer demand for a branded Intel product.
final.uncertainty: The size of the enthusiast market and their willingness to pay a premium for Intel are uncertain. The evidence does not address these directly.
would_change_if: If the survey shows enthusiasts willing to pay at least 20% more than general consumers, T2 would become more likely.
If a separate test shows strong demand from a specific use case (e.g., home networking) that OEMs do not currently serve, the investment could be reconsidered.
If new evidence shows Intel's brand is perceived as a differentiator by consumers, the case for a differentiated proposition would strengthen.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sensirion should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its CO2 and environmental sensors, based on evidence of market demand, technical feasibility, competitive landscape, and potential value capture.
constraints: Limited public information on Sensirion’s current consumer reach and sales; must rely on pre‑2021 sources.

alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑focused product for a specific use case (e.g., home air quality monitoring) and sell directly to individual buyers.

4) Partner with established consumer brands to embed Sensirion sensors in their products, leveraging the brand and distribution network.

X1.name: COVID vs Smart Home CO2 Device Test
X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups. Group A receives a portable CO2 device marketed as a health safety tool for COVID-era indoor air quality monitoring (price premium). Group B receives the same device marketed as part of a smart home energy efficiency bundle (price comparable to a standard smart home accessory). Both devices are offered through an online store with a 12‑week launch period.
X1.sample: 400 households recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups (200 per group). Recruitment targets homeowners aged 25‑55 with at least one child, and with a smart home device already owned.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as the percentage of households that place an order for the device within the 12‑week period. Secondary measure: self‑reported primary motivation (health safety vs smart home automation) via a post‑purchase survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show at least 15% higher purchase intent than Group B, because health‑safety messaging drives demand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show at least 15% higher purchase intent than Group A, because smart‑home positioning drives demand.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B’s by at least 15 percentage points, proceed to develop a health‑safety‑focused consumer proposition. If Group B’s purchase intent exceeds Group A’s by at least 15 percentage points, proceed to develop a smart‑home‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand for CO2 sensors, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed COVID vs Smart Home CO2 Device Test to measure purchase intent differences. If health‑safety messaging yields at least a 15‑point advantage, develop a differentiated health‑safety consumer proposition; otherwise, continue focusing on B2B markets.
final.target_customer: Homeowners aged 25‑55 with at least one child who already own a smart home device, targeting those who prioritize indoor air quality and health safety.
final.value_proposition: A portable CO2 device marketed as a COVID‑era health safety tool, leveraging Sensirion’s sensor technology to provide real‑time indoor air quality monitoring.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week online test with 400 households, measuring purchase intent and motivation. Use the 15‑point threshold to decide whether to proceed with a health‑safety proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and whether demand will persist beyond the pandemic remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether health‑safety messaging drives purchase more than smart‑home positioning.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B (smart‑home positioning) achieving at least a 15‑point higher purchase intent than Group A, we would shift focus to a smart‑home‑focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or a smaller difference than 15 points, we would recommend maintaining B2B focus and not committing to a consumer proposition.

arguments.sample: 400 households recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups (200 per group). Recruitment targets homeowners aged 25‑55 with at least one child, and with a smart home device already owned.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured as the percentage of households that place an order for the device within the 12‑week period. Secondary measure: self‑reported primary motivation (health safety vs smart home automation) via a post‑purchase survey.

If Group B’s purchase intent exceeds Group A’s by at least 15 percentage points, proceed to develop a smart‑home‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

X1.name: Price vs. Premium Positioning Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a price-focused or premium-focused description of the same LED bulb (EcoSmart LED Downlight). Participants are randomly assigned to either the price condition (bulb priced at $20, $30, or $40) or the premium condition (bulb positioned as offering industry-best light quality and energy efficiency at the same price). They are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults who have purchased a light bulb in the past year, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and income.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (on a 7‑point scale) for each condition and the difference in intent between conditions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the price condition, purchase intent will be higher than in the premium condition for all price points, and the difference will be statistically significant (e.g., mean intent in price condition ≥ 6.5 points higher than in premium condition).
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be higher than in the price condition for all price points, and the difference will be statistically significant (e.g., mean intent in premium condition ≥ 6.5 points higher than in price condition).

X1.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent in the premium condition is at least 6.5 points higher than in the price condition, proceed to develop a premium‑positioning consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 6.5 points, indicate that the premium positioning is not supported by evidence and recommend focusing on price‑driven demand.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer adoption drivers (price or quality). Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows LED bulbs are affordable and being embraced, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will adopt them primarily on price or that a premium positioning would drive higher demand. Conduct the proposed Price vs. Premium Positioning Test to determine whether price or quality drives purchase intent before committing to a consumer product.
final.target_customer: Consumers who purchase lighting for residential or small commercial use, particularly those who value energy efficiency and are price‑sensitive.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that either leverages low price and rebates (price‑driven) or positions LED bulbs as premium quality products (quality‑driven), depending on which test shows higher purchase intent.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €18,000 online survey test comparing price‑focused and premium‑focused messaging for the EcoSmart LED Downlight, with a decision rule of a ≥ 6.5 point difference in purchase intent between conditions.
final.uncertainty: The evidence does not resolve whether consumers will adopt LED bulbs primarily on price, quality, or other factors. The premium positioning claim is supported by a company‑assertion, not independent data.
would_change_if: If the test shows the premium condition yields a ≥ 6.5 point higher purchase intent than the price condition, we would shift toward a premium‑positioning strategy.
If the test shows no significant difference or the premium condition underperforms, we would recommend focusing on price‑driven demand or exploring a different route to consumers.

arguments.name: Price vs. Premium Positioning Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a price-focused or premium-focused description of the same LED bulb (EcoSmart LED Downlight). Participants are randomly assigned to either the price condition (bulb priced at $20, $30, or $40) or the premium condition (bulb positioned as offering industry-best light quality and energy efficiency at the same price). They are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults who have purchased a light bulb in the past year, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and income.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (on a 7‑point scale) for each condition and the difference in intent between conditions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the price condition, purchase intent will be higher than in the premium condition for all price points, and the difference will be statistically significant (e.g., mean intent in price condition ≥ 6.5 points higher than in premium condition).
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be higher than in the price condition for all price points, and the difference will be statistically significant (e.g., mean intent in premium condition ≥ 6.5 points higher than in price condition).

arguments.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent in the premium condition is at least 6.5 points higher than in the price condition, proceed to develop a premium‑positioning consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 6.5 points, indicate that the premium positioning is not supported by evidence and recommend focusing on price‑driven demand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows that LED bulbs are affordable and being embraced, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will adopt them primarily on price or that a premium positioning would drive higher demand. Conduct the proposed Price vs. Premium Positioning Test to determine whether price or quality drives purchase intent before committing to a consumer product

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in autumn 2009 to justify Probi investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its clinically documented probiotic strains (e.g., Lactobacillus plantarum 299v).
constraints: Limited to public sources published before autumn 2009; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, regulatory feasibility, and potential value capture for Probi.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not speculation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a direct‑to‑consumer (DTC) product line for a specific use case (e.g., gut health, immune support) sold through online channels.
2) License the same strains to consumer‑focused brands or retailers for co‑branding, capturing royalties.
3) Expand the existing B2B licensing model by targeting new dairy or food manufacturers, potentially increasing royalty revenue.
4) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B licensing and royalty income without creating a consumer proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging Perrigo’s existing Good Sense brand and OTC manufacturing capabilities. Begin with a small-scale test market to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for brand trust.

frame.objective: Determine whether Perrigo should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its over-the-counter medicine development and manufacturing capabilities, based on evidence available up to late 2014.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2014; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Consider Perrigo’s existing B2B supply contracts and its role as a generic manufacturer; must assess whether a consumer proposition would disrupt or enhance those relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., a branded OTC medication for a particular condition).
2) Expand into a new B2B segment by offering consumer products under Perrigo’s own brand to existing or new partners.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing OTC, generic, and B2B manufacturing without creating a consumer proposition.
4) License Perrigo’s OTC formulations to third‑party consumer brands for co‑branding and distribution.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if the product is positioned as a premium, brand‑driven solution for a specific, high‑need use case, because they trust established brand names and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
T1.who_benefits: Perrigo benefits by capturing higher margins and brand equity through premium pricing and increased consumer loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic to branded products when they perceive the brand as trustworthy and the product as addressing a specific, often painful, need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Perrigo can charge premium prices for the branded product, retain customers for repeat purchases, and potentially expand into adjacent use cases.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded product that offers a clear benefit over generic alternatives.
Perrigo can maintain quality and efficacy standards to support premium positioning.
Retail channels will allocate shelf space and promote the branded product effectively.
predictions: In a test market, a branded version of a specific use case (e.g., a skin care product) will achieve higher average order value and repeat purchase rates than a generic alternative.
Surveyed consumers will indicate higher trust in the brand and higher intent to recommend the branded product.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if the product is positioned as a premium, brand‑driven solution for a specific, high‑need use case, because they trust established brand names and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if the product is positioned as a convenient, convenient-to-buy solution for a specific use case, because they seek easy access to over-the-counter relief without the hassle of prescription or brand switching.
T2.who_benefits: Perrigo benefits by reaching consumers who already purchase OTC products, increasing overall OTC sales volume and potentially capturing additional margin through convenience-driven pricing.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers choose OTC products for their convenience and immediate availability, especially for acute or recurring conditions, leading them to prefer a single, familiar brand over multiple options.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Perrigo can increase unit sales by offering a branded product that is already familiar to consumers, and can command higher prices due to the convenience premium.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and ease of purchase over brand loyalty when choosing OTC products.
The specific use case (e.g., pain relief) is a frequent or recurring need that motivates purchase.
Retail channels will promote the convenience-driven product effectively.
predictions: In a test market, a convenience-focused branded product will achieve higher purchase rates and higher average order value compared to a generic alternative.
Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as the top reason for choosing the branded product.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if the product is positioned as a convenient, convenient-to-buy solution for a specific use case, because they seek easy access to over-the-counter relief without the hassle of prescription or brand switching.

X1.name: Brand vs Convenience Test for Good Sense
X1.method: Run a controlled online survey with a sample of 500 U.S. adults (aged 18-65) who have purchased OTC products in the past 6 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (Brand-Differentiated) and Condition B (Convenience-Differentiated). In Condition A, participants view a product description of a specific use case (e.g., skin irritation) and are asked to indicate whether they would buy it at a premium price. In Condition B, participants view the same product description and are asked to indicate whether they would buy it at a convenience price (e.g., $2.99). Both conditions present the same product but with different positioning. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (dollar amount).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults who have purchased OTC products in the past 6 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (dollar amount) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B, because consumers are motivated by brand trust and premium positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A, because consumers prioritize convenience and ease of purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least $1.50, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (brand positioning). If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least $1.50, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition. If the difference is less than $1.50, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and focus on existing B2B relationships.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer willingness to pay a premium for a branded product. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts consumer adoption based on brand trust and premium positioning.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging Perrigo’s existing Good Sense brand and OTC manufacturing capabilities. Begin with a small-scale test market to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for brand trust.
final.target_customer: Consumers who purchase OTC products for specific, often painful, conditions and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality and brand trust.
final.value_proposition: A branded OTC product positioned as a premium, trusted solution for a specific use case, offering higher margins and brand loyalty compared to generic alternatives.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Brand vs Convenience Test (500 U.S. adults, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under brand-differentiated and convenience-differentiated conditions.
final.uncertainty: The size of the premium willingness to pay and the extent to which consumers will switch from generic to branded products remain uncertain. Evidence on consumer trust and brand perception is limited to company claims and does not prove real
would_change_if: If the test shows a willingness-to-pay difference of less than €1.50 between brand and convenience positioning, indicating insufficient premium motivation, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of maintaining B2B relationships.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience-driven OTC products, the recommendation would shift toward a convenience-focused proposition.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Evidence shows SKF already sells lubrication systems globally and has a large distributor network, but no public source demonstrates consumer demand for premium SKF lubrication. A proposed test (Consumer Messaging Test) is needed to measure willingness to pay for performance versus brand trust.

frame.objective: Determine whether SKF should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current SKF revenue is $9.3B FY2024, primarily from automotive, aerospace, industrial OEMs and aftermarket distributors.
Uncertainty about SKF’s current reach to individual buyers; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that SKF can capture.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home DIY, small business, or niche industrial).
2) Expand the existing B2B distribution network to reach individual buyers directly via online channels or new retail partnerships.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on OEMs and aftermarket distributors.
4) License SKF technology to consumer brands for consumer‑grade products (e.g., bearings for outdoor equipment).
5) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop and market consumer‑focused products under a joint brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt SKF consumer-grade lubrication products if they perceive superior durability and performance compared to generic lubricants, because they need reliable protection for rotating equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners of tools, machinery, and outdoor equipment who require long-lasting lubrication.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If SKF can demonstrate that its lubricants offer higher wear resistance and longer service life, consumers will switch from cheaper alternatives to SKF products.
T1.how_value_is_captured: SKF can charge a premium price for premium lubricants and sell through retail channels, capturing margin on higher-margin consumer products.
assumptions: Consumer awareness of SKF's industrial reputation exists.
Retail distribution channels can reach individual buyers.
Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived performance benefits.
predictions: A survey of DIY enthusiasts will show a willingness to pay at least 20% more for SKF lubricants than for generic alternatives.
Sales of SKF consumer lubricants will increase in regions where SKF's industrial reputation is well-known.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Performance vs Brand Trust
X1.method: Online survey with two randomized message arms. Participants are recruited from DIY and small business demographics. Arm A receives a performance message emphasizing SKF's superior durability and wear resistance. Arm B receives a brand trust message emphasizing SKF's industrial reputation and trust. Both arms offer the same SKF consumer lubrication product at a premium price (e.g., 20% above generic). Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 seen Arm A, 250 seen Arm B, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and purchase intent (7-point scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Arm B, because performance messaging directly addresses durability concerns.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Arm A, because brand trust messaging directly addresses trust concerns.

X1.decision_rule: If Arm A average WTP is at least 15% higher than Arm B (e.g., €15.50 vs €13.30), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on performance. If Arm B average WTP is at least 15% higher, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on brand trust. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not invest.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for SKF lubrication products. Therefore it does not affect T1.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify L.M. Ericsson investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current 4G/5G networks, cloud software, and managed services.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider Ericsson’s existing B2B/enterprise focus and current consumer reach.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home networking, IoT for residential users).
2) Expand existing managed services and cloud software offerings to new B2B segments (e.g., small and medium‑size enterprises).
3) No expansion – maintain current portfolio and focus on existing markets.
4) Partner with or acquire a consumer brand to leverage existing consumer assets (e.g., Ericsson’s smartwatch or home networking).
5) Target a new geographic or regulatory segment (e.g., emerging markets with high mobile penetration) without altering core offerings.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated home networking proposition because they increasingly view home connectivity as a personal convenience and status signal, leading them to purchase dedicated devices rather than rely on existing smartphones or tablets.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking dedicated home networking for streaming, IoT, and smart home integration.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting perception from a utility to a lifestyle and status item makes consumers willing to pay a premium for a dedicated device.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ericsson can capture value through premium-priced hardware, subscription services for advanced features, and brand differentiation in a crowded consumer market.
assumptions: Consumers currently use smartphones for home networking and would switch to a dedicated device.
Status and lifestyle are significant drivers of purchase decisions for home networking.
Ericsson can differentiate its offering through design, brand positioning, and service integration.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a dedicated home networking device compared to a smartphone-based solution.
Purchase intent will be higher among consumers who self-identify as lifestyle-conscious versus those who prioritize functionality.
Sales of a differentiated home networking product will be concentrated in regions where lifestyle branding resonates (e.g., Western Europe, North America).
T1.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated home networking proposition because they increasingly view home connectivity as a personal convenience and status signal, leading them to purchase dedicated devices rather than rely on existing smartphones or tablets.

T2.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated home networking proposition because they face increasing connectivity demands (IoT devices, smart home integration) and lack a single, integrated solution, leading them to seek a dedicated device that simplifies management.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers with multiple IoT devices and smart home systems who need a unified networking experience.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The complexity of managing multiple devices and protocols motivates consumers to purchase a single, integrated solution that simplifies connectivity and reduces setup time.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ericsson can capture value through a bundled hardware and software offering, subscription services for advanced management, and recurring revenue from service upgrades.
assumptions: Consumers currently struggle with managing multiple IoT devices and smart home systems.
A single, integrated solution would reduce the time and effort required to set up and manage home networking.
Ericsson can differentiate its offering through ease of use, integration with existing ecosystems, and competitive pricing.
predictions: Consumers will report higher satisfaction with a bundled home networking solution compared to purchasing separate devices.
Purchase intent will be higher among consumers who own multiple IoT devices and smart home systems.
Sales of a bundled home networking product will be concentrated in regions with high IoT adoption (e.g., North America, Western Europe).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Wärtsilä investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current marine engines, propulsion, lifecycle services, engine power plants, and battery storage for utilities.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current sales are to marine customers, energy providers, utilities, and developers, not to individual consumers.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential solar storage, RV propulsion, or home energy storage).
2) Expand the existing marine and utility business without a differentiated consumer proposition (maintain current B2B focus).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B markets (marine, utilities, energy storage).
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute a consumer product (e.g., a consumer‑branded battery storage kit).
5) License Wärtsilä’s technology to consumer OEMs or retailers for consumer‑branded products.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Wärtsilä’s energy storage technology primarily when it is positioned as a premium, safety‑certified home backup power solution, because they value reliability and compliance with safety standards.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners seeking reliable backup power for critical loads.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive Wärtsilä’s safety certification and reliability as superior to generic or lower‑cost alternatives, they will be willing to pay a premium price for a product that meets their safety and performance expectations.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Wärtsil can capture value by selling premium‑priced energy storage systems directly to consumers through its own brand, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and safety credentials to justify higher prices.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of and trust safety certification in energy storage products.
Safety certification is a decisive factor in consumer purchasing decisions for backup power.
Wärtsil’s brand reputation in marine and utility sectors transfers to consumer perception.
predictions: In a test offering a Wärtsilä consumer‑branded energy storage system at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a comparable low‑cost alternative.
Surveyed consumers will rank safety certification as the top reason for choosing Wärtsilä over competitors.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Wärtsilä’s energy storage technology primarily when it is positioned as a premium, safety‑certified home backup power solution, because they value reliability and compliance with safety standards.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Wärtsilä’s energy storage technology primarily when it is positioned as a scalable, modular solution for multiple use cases (e.g., home backup, RV propulsion, or commercial applications), because they seek flexibility and cost‑efficiency across different applications.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners, RV owners, and small‑business owners who need adaptable energy storage for various needs.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive Wärtsilä’s modular design and scalability as superior to single‑purpose or proprietary systems, they will be willing to purchase a system that can be applied across multiple scenarios, reducing overall cost and effort.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Wärtsil can capture value by offering a modular energy storage platform that can be sold under different consumer‑branded names, leveraging its existing B2B expertise to justify higher upfront costs while maintaining margin through volume.
assumptions: Consumers value flexibility and the ability to use a single product for multiple applications.
Modular design reduces total cost of ownership compared to specialized single‑purpose systems.
Wärtsil’s technical capability supports modular integration without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a modular Wärtsilä energy storage system at a comparable price to specialized alternatives, adoption rates will be higher than for a single‑purpose system.
Surveyed consumers will rank modularity and cross‑application use as the top reason for choosing Wärtsilä over competitors.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Modular Positioning
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a premium‑positioned Wärtsilä home backup power system (safety‑certified, premium price) or a modular‑positioned system (same technical specifications, sold under different consumer‑branded names). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 adults in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and self‑reported interest in home energy storage.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the premium‑positioned system will report higher purchase intent and safety certification as the top reason compared to the modular‑positioned system.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the modular‑positioned system will report higher purchase intent and modularity/cross‑application use as the top reason compared to the premium‑positioned system.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium‑positioned system’s purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than the modular‑positioned system’s score, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If the modular‑positioned system’s score is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a modular consumer proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not invest in either proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, safety certification, or willingness to pay for a premium home backup power solution. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence does not show consumer demand for premium safety‑certified home backup power, nor does it address scalability or modularity. The proposed test is pending.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners seeking reliable backup power for critical loads.
final.value_proposition: A premium, safety‑certified home backup power system leveraging Wärtsilä’s marine and utility reputation to justify higher prices.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (premium vs modular positioning) to measure purchase intent and top reason for choosing the product.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for safety certification and the extent to which Wärtsilä’s brand reputation transfers to consumers are unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows the premium‑positioned system’s purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than the modular‑positioned system’s score, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition.
If additional evidence shows strong consumer demand for safety certification and willingness to pay a premium, reconsider the premium proposition.
If the test shows the modular‑positioned system’s purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a modular consumer proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Brand vs Performance Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from homeowners and small fabricators interested in home welding projects. They view a product description of a consumer‑grade Lincoln welding torch and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑no intent, 7‑definitive purchase). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Brand‑focused (emphasizing professional reliability and trust) or Performance‑focused (emphasizing high‑performance capabilities and durability).
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) from the US, recruited via an online panel targeting homeowners and small fabricators who have completed a home welding project.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score on a 7‑point scale for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Brand‑focused condition will achieve a mean purchase intent score at least 1.5 points higher than Performance‑focused condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Performance‑focused condition will achieve a mean purchase intent score at least 1.5 points higher than Brand‑focused condition.

X1.decision_rule: If Brand‑focused mean score ≥ 5.5 and Performance‑focused mean score ≤ 4.0, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing brand trust and professional reliability. If Performance‑focused mean score ≥ 5.5 and Brand‑focused mean score ≤ 4.0, develop a consumer proposition emphasizing performance and durability. If neither condition meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Health vs Lifestyle Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and choice-based conjoint. Participants are recruited from homeowners with known indoor air quality concerns (health group) and tech-savvy homeowners without concerns (lifestyle group). Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for a Vaisala air quality monitor: health-focused (emphasizing indoor air quality monitoring and health safety) and lifestyle-focused (emphasizing smart home integration, convenience, and status). After viewing the description, participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The test also measures willingness to subscribe to a data service for 12 months.
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 health group, 150 lifestyle group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home ownership status.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1-7) for each message. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health group will have higher average purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than lifestyle group, indicating demand driven by health necessity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle group will have higher average purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than health group, indicating demand driven by lifestyle and status.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the health message is at least 1.5 points higher than for the lifestyle message (i.e., health intent >= lifestyle intent + 1.5), proceed to develop a health-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, proceed to develop a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home testing kits) that emphasizes laboratory-grade quality and reliability. Begin with a small-scale test to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for professional-grade accuracy.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sartorius should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current revenue is €3.538.1m (2025) with 85% from life science customers.
Uncertainty about Sartorius’s current reach to individual buyers.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home testing kits, DIY lab consumables).
2) Expand into adjacent B2B segments with existing products (e.g., add consumer-friendly versions of Lab balances or pipettes).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on life science customers.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering product offering.
5) Target a new customer group with existing products (e.g., small businesses, educational institutions) rather than a new use case.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Sartorius products for home testing if they perceive them as high-quality, reliable laboratory-grade tools, because they trust professional-grade instruments for accuracy and safety.
T1.who_benefits: Home testers and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable results for health monitoring.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers see Sartorius products as the same quality as lab equipment, they will be willing to pay a premium for accuracy and safety, leading to repeat purchases.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sartorius can charge premium prices for consumer-grade versions and sell through retail channels, capturing margin on higher-margin products.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for laboratory-grade accuracy.
Sartorius can adapt existing product lines to meet consumer safety standards.
Retail distribution channels will accept consumer-grade versions of lab equipment.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-friendly version of a lab instrument, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic consumer product.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a comparable consumer product.
Repeat purchase rate will be higher for the consumer-friendly version than for a standard consumer product.

T2.who_benefits: Consumers who value credibility and safety in health-related products.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers see Sartorius as a brand used by professionals, they will trust its products more and be willing to purchase them, even at a premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sartorius can position its consumer offerings as professional-grade, leveraging its existing reputation to command higher prices and build brand loyalty.
assumptions: Consumers associate professional-grade brands with higher quality and safety.
Sartorius can effectively communicate its professional reputation to consumers.
The brand perception can be transferred across product categories.
predictions: In a test where the brand is framed as professional-grade, purchase intent will be higher than when the brand is framed as consumer-focused.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a comparable consumer product.
Brand awareness will be higher for the professional-grade framing than for the consumer-focused framing.

X1.name: Consumer Framing Test for Home Testing Kit
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product framing. Participants view a mock Sartorius home testing kit (e.g., a digital thermometer) and are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. They are then asked about brand perception (professional-grade vs consumer-focused).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers interested in home health monitoring, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by age and gender to reflect target demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score and maximum willingness to pay for the framed product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when the product is framed as professional-grade (lab‑grade).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when the product is framed as consumer‑focused (brand trust).

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the professional‑grade framing exceeds the consumer‑focused framing by ≥ 1.5 points on the 10‑point scale, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer perception of Sartorius products for home testing. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home testing kits) that emphasizes laboratory-grade quality and reliability. Begin with a small-scale test to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for professional-grade accuracy.
final.target_customer: Home testers and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable results for health monitoring.
final.value_proposition: Sartorius can offer consumer-friendly versions of its existing lab instruments, positioned as high-quality, professional-grade tools for home use, allowing premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Framing Test (300 participants, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under professional-grade versus consumer-focused framing.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for Sartorius products and the actual willingness to pay a premium for laboratory-grade accuracy remain uncertain. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the professional-grade framing is at least 1.5 points lower than for the consumer-focused framing, we would reconsider the investment.

If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for Sartorius products already exists (e.g., existing e-commerce sales or retail partnerships), we would shift focus to expanding the current B2B reach rather than creating a new consumer line.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home infusion therapy if they view it as a convenient, safe, and discreet way to manage chronic pain at home, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust.
T1.who_benefits: Patients with chronic pain seeking convenience and discretion; B. Braun would capture value through premium pricing and recurring revenue from consumables.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of home infusion as a viable option for chronic pain management, coupled with a desire for convenience and discretion, will shift consumer preference from hospital-based care to home-based solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: B. Braun can sell consumables directly to consumers at higher margins, offer subscription models for ongoing supply, and leverage its trusted brand to command premium prices.
assumptions: Consumers trust B. Braun's brand for medical devices.
Home infusion therapy is perceived as safe and effective by patients.
Consumers are willing to pay more for a branded, convenient solution.
predictions: Surveyed patients will indicate high intent to purchase home infusion devices if priced at a premium.
Sales of B. Braun's consumer-facing consumables will increase in regions where home infusion is promoted.
Willingness to pay for a subscription service for ongoing supplies will be higher than for a one-time purchase.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home infusion therapy if they view it as a convenient, safe, and discreet way to manage chronic pain at home, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home infusion therapy if they experience it firsthand through a trial program, reducing perceived risk and increasing trust in the product, leading to higher purchase intent.
T2.who_benefits: Patients with chronic pain who are hesitant to commit to a new therapy; B. Braun would capture value through higher conversion rates from trial to purchase and recurring revenue from consumables.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Firsthand experience mitigates uncertainty about safety, effectiveness, and ease of use, making consumers more likely to purchase a product they have tested themselves.
T2.how_value_is_captured: B. Braun can offer trial kits or subscription-based supply with a refund policy, generating revenue from consumables while building brand trust through direct consumer engagement.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a modest upfront cost for a trial kit.

B. Braun can deliver a safe and effective trial experience.

Customers who purchase a trial kit will have a higher conversion rate to a full purchase than those who do not.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Infusion
X1.method: Online randomized controlled trial with three message conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of patients with chronic pain. Each participant sees one of three ad messages for a home infusion kit: (A) convenience and discretion (highlighting ease of use and discreet delivery); (B) safety and trust (highlighting B. Braun's leadership in safety and efficacy); (C) trial experience (highlighting a free trial kit to experience the product firsthand). Participants then indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium price.
X1.sample: 300 adult patients with chronic pain, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three message conditions (100 per condition).
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) across the three conditions. Secondary measure: willingness to pay premium (difference in premium intent between conditions).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will generate the highest average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay, as it emphasizes convenience and discretion.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition C will generate the highest average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay, as it emphasizes firsthand experience and reduces perceived risk.

X1.decision_rule: If average purchase intent in Condition A is at least 1.5 points higher than in Condition C and the difference in premium willingness to pay is at least €10, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and discretion. If Condition C’s intent is at least 1.5 points higher than Condition A and the premium difference is at least €10, proceed with a trial‑based proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or purchase behavior for home infusion therapy. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home infusion therapy that emphasizes convenience, discretion, and safety, supported by a willingness-to-pay test. If the test confirms a premium price point and higher purchase intent for convenience messaging, proceed with a direct-to-consumer or subscription model. If not, consider a trial-based approach first.
final.target_customer: Patients with chronic pain who seek convenient, discreet, and safe home management of their condition.
final.value_proposition: A branded home infusion kit that delivers discreet, easy-to-use therapy at home, leveraging B. Braun's trusted brand to justify premium pricing and recurring revenue from consumables.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (300 patients, three message conditions, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and premium willingness to pay. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home infusion therapy, actual willingness to pay for a premium product, and the effectiveness of a trial-based approach remain uncertain. Evidence from the test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows Condition C (trial experience) generates higher purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Condition A (convenience), we would shift to a trial-based proposition.
If the test fails to meet the thresholds for either condition, we would conclude that a consumer proposition is not justified at this time.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand for residential ventilation, and the framing test is needed to validate purchase intent. If the test shows health‑framed framing generates significantly higher intent than comfort‑framed framing, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether Halton should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify Halton’s current reach to individual buyers and its existing consumer products.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that would generate revenue for Halton.
Any recommendation must consider Halton’s existing six business areas (commercial kitchens, ships, healthcare, cleanrooms, energy, infrastructure) and its current B2B focus.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home air quality, portable ventilation for residential buildings).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio by adding new industrial or commercial applications without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets and existing product lines.
4) Change the route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with retailers, offer subscription services, target new demographics) without altering the core product.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of indoor air quality issues (e.g., mold, dust, pollutants) creates a perceived health risk that motivates purchase of solutions that improve air quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Halton can charge premium prices for its advanced ventilation systems and capture recurring revenue through maintenance and service contracts.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to invest in indoor air quality solutions for health reasons.
Halton's technical capabilities can be effectively communicated to residential buyers.
Regulatory or health guidelines will continue to emphasize indoor air quality.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will express higher purchase intent for Halton's residential products when framed as a health necessity compared to general comfort or energy efficiency.
Willingness to pay will be higher for residential units than for commercial units when health benefits are highlighted.

X1.name: Framing Test for Residential Ventilation Purchase Intent
X1.method: Online survey with randomized framing condition.
X1.sample: 300 homeowners (150 per condition) recruited via a panel to match Halton's current B2B customer demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑0 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR) for a hypothetical Halton residential ventilation unit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when framed as a health necessity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when framed as energy-efficient and comfort-enhancing.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in the health‑framed condition exceeds the intent in the comfort‑framed condition by ≥ 10 points and both conditions are statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. Otherwise, do not invest.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer perception of health necessity or demand for residential ventilation. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand for residential ventilation, and a framing test is needed to validate purchase intent. If the test shows health‑framed framing generates significantly higher intent than comfort‑framed framing, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with respiratory concerns, allergy sufferers, and health‑conscious consumers who perceive indoor air quality as a medical necessity.
final.value_proposition: Advanced residential ventilation systems marketed as a health necessity solution, offering improved indoor air quality and potential health benefits, with premium pricing and recurring maintenance services.
final.next_action: Run the proposed framing test (300 homeowners, randomized conditions, purchase intent and willingness to pay) to determine whether health‑framed messaging drives higher demand than comfort‑framed messaging.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for residential ventilation is uncertain; the test is needed to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay. Market size and competitive landscape are also unknown.
would_change_if: If the framing test shows comfort‑framed messaging generates significantly higher purchase intent than health‑framed messaging, or if market research reveals a large, underserved segment of health‑conscious homeowners.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for residential ventilation, such as data on purchase intent, market size, or competitive positioning.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home automation, targeting homeowners who value industrial-grade reliability and integration with smart home ecosystems. Begin with a limited pilot offering a branded consumer product at a 20% premium over generic smart home devices to test demand and price sensitivity.

frame.objective: Determine whether Bosch Rexroth should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for end users.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home automation, outdoor recreation, or small‑scale industrial applications).
2) Expand the existing ctrlX AUTOMATION platform to serve individual users directly via a new sales channel (e.g., online marketplace, subscription).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B machinery manufacturers and end‑users.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop products for a specific use case (e.g., Bosch Rexroth‑branded consumer tools).
5) License core technologies to consumer product manufacturers rather than selling branded consumer products.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt Bosch Rexroth products for home automation because they value industrial-grade reliability and integration with existing smart home ecosystems, leading them to purchase premium-priced, branded solutions.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking reliable, integrated automation for tasks like cooking, cleaning, or storage.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from off-the-shelf smart home devices to branded, industrial-grade products they trust for durability and seamless connectivity.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Bosch Rexroth can charge premium prices for branded consumer products and potentially offer subscription services for software updates or monitoring.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for industrial-grade reliability.
Smart home ecosystems (e.g., Apple HomeKit, Google Nest) are sufficient to drive demand.
Bosch Rexroth can reach consumers through retail or online channels without heavy marketing spend.
predictions: In a test offering a branded consumer product at a 20% premium over generic smart home devices, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a generic device.
Surveyed consumers will cite reliability and integration with existing smart home ecosystems as primary purchase drivers.
T1.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt Bosch Rexroth products for home automation because they value industrial-grade reliability and integration with existing smart home ecosystems, leading them to purchase premium-priced, branded solutions.

T2.claim: Individual consumers will adopt Bosch Rexroth products for outdoor recreation (e.g., camping, gardening) because they need durable, efficient tools that perform in rugged conditions, leading them to purchase branded outdoor equipment.
T2.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and hobbyists who require reliable tools for tasks like cutting, moving, or packaging.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic outdoor tools to branded products they trust for durability and performance in challenging environments.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Bosch Rexroth can charge premium prices for outdoor-specific products and potentially offer accessories or maintenance services.
assumptions: Outdoor consumers prioritize durability and performance over cost.
Bosch Rexroth's industrial reputation transfers to outdoor applications.
There is a measurable market for outdoor-specific automation tools.
predictions: In a test offering a branded outdoor tool at a 20% premium over generic outdoor tools, purchase intent among outdoor enthusiasts will be at least 15% higher than for a generic tool.
Surveyed consumers will cite durability and performance as primary purchase drivers.
T2.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt Bosch Rexroth products for outdoor recreation (e.g., camping, gardening) because they need durable, efficient tools that perform in rugged conditions, leading them to purchase branded outdoor equipment.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Home Automation vs Outdoor Tools
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a branded consumer product (home automation or outdoor tool) and a generic alternative. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 adults (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target consumers (homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (percentage of participants rating ≥ 7 out of 10) and average maximum price willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher average price for the home automation product compared to the generic alternative.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher average price for the outdoor tool product compared to the generic alternative.

X1.decision_rule: If the home automation product achieves purchase intent ≥ 15% and its average price is at least 20% above the generic alternative, proceed to develop a consumer proposition for home automation. If the outdoor tool product achieves purchase intent ≥ 15% and its average price is at least 20% above the generic alternative, develop a consumer proposition for outdoor tools. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for home automation or outdoor tools. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.target_customer: Homeowners seeking reliable, integrated automation for tasks like cooking, cleaning, or storage.
final.value_proposition: Industrial-grade reliability and seamless integration with existing smart home ecosystems, positioned as a premium, branded solution for home automation.

final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for home automation and willingness to pay a premium are unknown. The test will resolve this, but evidence of actual purchase behavior is needed.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 15% or price willingness below 20% of the generic alternative, the investment would be reconsidered.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for outdoor tools or other use cases, the recommendation would shift accordingly.
